description: Width tiers for Health and Physical Education Years 1-2 — all 11 descriptors across Moving our bodies, Making active choices, Learning through movement, Identities and change, Interacting with others, and Making healthy and safe choices strands.
subject: Health and Physical Education

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest honest application of the descriptor's command term. For movement descriptors, the minimum is a single movement context or activity type in which the skill or strategy is practised. For health descriptors, the minimum is the narrowest set of phenomena or situations that honestly satisfies the descriptor's verb (identify, describe, investigate, practise). Minimum is not what is easy — it is what the command term requires.
width_notes.typical_width: The full scope of the descriptor as reflected in ACARA elaborations — the range of contexts, activity types, situations or phenomena a well-taught class would engage with. Does not require every elaboration to be covered, but reflects the spirit and scope of the descriptor.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add new activity contexts, cultural settings, situations or phenomena. Must genuinely broaden the range of experience rather than offering harder versions of the same context. First Nations directions are included by default where elaborations indicate them.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations are used as source data for grounding typical_width and identifying wider directions. They are not a checklist — some are merged where they describe the same activity at different specificity. Wider items may extend beyond elaborations where clearly within the descriptor's scope and year band.

AC9HP2M01.minimum_width: Practise at least two fundamental movement skills (locomotor and/or object control) in one movement situation; attempt to apply them purposefully.
AC9HP2M01.typical_width: Practise a range of fundamental movement skills — locomotor, balance, and object control — across multiple movement situations including minor games, sequences, and water or outdoor activities; apply skills purposefully in each context.
wider: Practise gliding and kicking movements in water and compare how the same locomotor principles apply differently in an aquatic context
Participate in children's games from First Nations Australian cultures and identify which fundamental movement skills are used and how
Invent a movement sequence combining locomotor, balance and object control elements and evaluate how successfully the skills were applied
elaborations: performing locomotor movements using different body parts to travel in different directions
selecting and implementing different movement skills to be successful in a range of games
performing fundamental movement skills involving controlling objects with equipment and different parts of the body
practising gliding forward and backward in the water using arm and kicking movements
demonstrating balances and describing what helps to maintain stable positions

AC9HP2M02.minimum_width: Investigate at least two different ways of moving or manipulating objects; draw a conclusion about which was more effective and give one reason.
AC9HP2M02.typical_width: Investigate a range of movement approaches (varying speed, direction, level) and object/space manipulation strategies; draw conclusions about effectiveness using observations from multiple activity and game contexts.
wider: Invent a new game based on familiar rules and equipment, and evaluate whether the movement choices and rules make it interesting and challenging
Use stimuli (music, rhythm, words) to create simple playground games and compare which stimulus produces the most varied or effective movement
Investigate moving around different outdoor spaces and draw conclusions about which movement types are most appropriate for safe and efficient navigation
elaborations: demonstrating changes in speed, direction and level as they use locomotor and non-locomotor skills in sequences

inventing new games, based on rules and equipment from familiar games, and drawing conclusions about whether the rules and choice of equipment provide for an interesting, challenging and enjoyable game
using stimuli such as equipment, rhythm, music and words to create simple playground games and assessing which games they enjoy most
using different types of equipment to create an original game or solve a movement challenge and evaluating the game or solution against a set of criteria
participating in activities that require students to move around different outdoor spaces and discussing which types of movement are most appropriate to move around safely and efficiently

AC9HP2M03.minimum_width: Participate in at least one physical activity in an outdoor or natural setting; identify at least one factor that made it enjoyable.
AC9HP2M03.typical_width: Participate in a range of physical activities in natural and outdoor settings, including minor games; identify and investigate factors that make each enjoyable and compare indoor and outdoor settings.
wider: Participate in children's games from First Nations Australian cultures (such as Keentan played by the Kalkadoon People) and compare enjoyment factors with familiar games
Investigate physical features of multiple natural and outdoor settings and draw conclusions about which features enable or limit which types of physical activity
Survey classmates about their enjoyment factors and identify which factors are widely shared versus personal — and discuss what this means for planning physical activities
elaborations: recognising the physical features in a range of different environments, including natural and outdoor settings, that make physical activity in these spaces enjoyable

participating in children's games from First Nations Australian cultures, such as Keentan played by the Kalkadoon People of the north-west central districts of Queensland, and discussing similarities with other games and activities they enjoy
participating in a range of minor games and exploring which ones they enjoy and what makes them enjoyable
comparing the characteristics and benefits of physical activities that can take place in an outdoor setting to those that take place inside

AC9HP2M04.minimum_width: Apply at least one rule in a physical activity and explain how it contributes to fair play; co-construct or agree to one rule modification with others.
AC9HP2M04.typical_width: Co-construct and apply rules across a range of physical activities; explain how specific rules promote fair play and demonstrate turn-taking and equipment sharing in group activities.
wider: Design a complete rule set for a new game that ensures equitable participation for all players, including those with different abilities or skill levels
Compare rules across two different types of activities and identify the common fair-play principle they both serve
Investigate rules from a First Nations Australian game and compare the fair-play principles they embody with rules from familiar games
elaborations: discussing changes to rules that will make an activity fairer or more inclusive of all learners
explaining how rules contribute to fair play and applying them in group activities
demonstrating turn-taking and sharing equipment when participating in play and minor games

AC9HP2M05.minimum_width: In at least one physical activity, apply a collaborative strategy (e.g. cooperating with a partner, including another person) and describe what they did.
AC9HP2M05.typical_width: Apply a range of collaborative strategies across different physical activities — partner practice, inclusion of others, game modification for all — and explain how each strategy supports collaborative participation.
wider: Propose and trial a game modification that specifically addresses an inclusion barrier experienced by a classmate, and evaluate whether the modification worked
Work with a partner from a different cultural or ability background and reflect on how to adjust collaborative strategies to suit different partners
Compare collaborative strategies that work in paired activities with those that work in small-group activities, and discuss what changes and why
elaborations: working cooperatively with a partner when practising new skills
describing and demonstrating how to include others in physical activities
proposing and trialling how a game can be changed so that everyone can be included

AC9HP2P01.minimum_width: Describe at least two personal qualities of their own and explain how one of them contributes to their identity.
AC9HP2P01.typical_width: Describe a range of personal qualities in themselves and others; explain how personal and cultural identities are influenced by groups and communities they belong to, using multiple examples.
wider: Explore how belonging to First Nations Australian cultural groups contributes to identities and how cultural practices shape personal qualities
Examine examples from Australians of Asian heritage that recognise how family and friends contribute to identity formation
Describe personal achievements in physical activities and explain how these experiences influenced their personal identity
elaborations: describing the personal qualities of characters in stories and how they are similar to and different from their own
describing how belonging to First Nations Australian cultural groups contributes to identities
exploring examples of cultural practices, including those of Australians of Asian heritage, that recognise the contributions of family and friends to identities
explaining how personal and cultural identities are influenced by the groups and communities to which we belong
participating in physical activities and describing how their own and others' personal qualities contribute to successful outcomes
describing personal achievements and sharing how they felt and how it influenced their personal identities

AC9HP2P02.minimum_width: Identify at least one skill or strategy for developing respectful relationships and demonstrate it in one context.
AC9HP2P02.typical_width: Identify and explore a range of skills and strategies for respectful relationships — including appropriate verbal language, body language, and inclusion strategies — across different social and movement contexts.
wider: Explore strategies for showing respect to First Nations Australians and acknowledging difference using appropriate language
Compare how strategies for respectful interaction look different across physical activity versus classroom or social contexts
Investigate characters in texts who demonstrate respect for different types of families and discuss what this reveals about respectful relationship strategies
elaborations: identifying characters in texts who demonstrate respect and cooperation to develop respectful relationships
identifying characters in texts who demonstrate respect for different types of families and carers, including those of different cultures, abilities or compositions

demonstrating appropriate language (including verbal, non-verbal, body language and gestures) when encouraging and including others in physical activities, when completing movement tasks or practising for performance
discussing strategies we can use to show respect to First Nations Australians and acknowledge difference using appropriate language
describing behaviours that may cause hurt or harm to others, or cause them to feel disrespected, including verbal and physical forms of bullying

AC9HP2P03.minimum_width: Identify at least one situation that triggers a strong emotional response and describe what the response looks like and how it might affect others.
AC9HP2P03.typical_width: Identify a range of situations that influence emotional responses in themselves and others; recognise emotional cues; describe self-regulation strategies for managing how emotions are expressed.
wider: Use role play and imaginative play to identify how someone might feel, think and act during an emergency — connecting situational triggers to response patterns
Explore how cultural context affects how emotions are expressed and what self-regulation strategies are culturally appropriate
Compare how the same situation might produce different emotional responses in different people and discuss the implications for understanding others
elaborations: recognising own emotions and demonstrating ways to manage how they express their emotions in different situations
exploring self-regulation strategies to manage emotional responses
identifying situations that may trigger strong emotional responses in themselves and others, and recognising the impact the responses can have on others
identifying how someone might feel, think and act during an emergency through role-play and imaginative play
predicting how a person or character might be feeling based on the words they use, their facial expressions and body language
recognising how self and others are feeling in a range of situations

AC9HP2P04.minimum_width: In a practised scenario, use one verbal and one non-verbal strategy to seek, give or deny permission; practise at least one context involving saying no to inappropriate touching.
AC9HP2P04.typical_width: Practise a range of strategies for seeking, giving and denying permission across multiple contexts; interact with others in a fair and respectful way regardless of differences in gender, abilities, race or personality.
wider: Compare permission strategies across different contexts (sharing equipment, physical contact, personal space) and evaluate which strategies are most effective in each
Practise permission and interaction strategies with peers of different abilities and backgrounds and reflect on how to adjust approaches
Explore situations where non-verbal cues alone may not be sufficient and discuss when assertive verbal communication is essential
elaborations: practising strategies they can use when they need to give or refuse consent; for example, saying yes and no in an assertive manner, using non-verbal body cues and gestures
practising ways to interact with others in a fair and respectful way in play and other activities, regardless of differences in gender, abilities, race or personality
exploring situations where they need to seek, give or deny permission and practising strategies to assert themselves; for example, saying no to inappropriate touching

AC9HP2P05.minimum_width: Name at least one trusted adult and one safe place; identify and rehearse at least one protective behaviour; describe at least one strategy for digital tool safety.
AC9HP2P05.typical_width: Identify and rehearse protective behaviours and help-seeking strategies across physical and digital contexts; identify a network of trusted people and safe places; explain why seeking help when problems are too big to solve alone is important.
wider: Explore how to seek help in different scenarios — at school, at home, and in public — and evaluate which strategies are most appropriate in each context
Role-play using protective behaviours in scenarios drawn from stories, everyday life, and online contexts, and compare the strategies used in each
Investigate how to recognise safe places in the local community using signs, symbols and physical markers
elaborations: identifying the body's reaction to a range of situations, including safe and unsafe situations, and comparing the different emotional responses
identifying and rehearsing strategies they can use when requiring assistance, such as asking an adult they trust, reading signs and symbols to identify safe places, and solving a problem with friends
proposing strategies they can use at school and home that promote healthy use of digital tools
recognising photos and locations of safe places and a network of people who can help
discussing the importance of seeking help when problems are too big to solve by themselves
exploring how characters in texts use protective behaviours and help-seeking strategies to keep themselves and others safe

AC9HP2P06.minimum_width: Identify at least two health messages or symbols in the community (e.g. poison labels, food guides) and explain their purpose; describe how eating a variety of fresh foods influences health.
AC9HP2P06.typical_width: Investigate a range of health messages and practices in the community — food labelling and marketing, medicine safety, digital tool rules, sustainability practices — and discuss the health purpose of each.
wider: Explore sustainable practices that can be implemented in the classroom (composting, edible gardens, reducing single-use plastics) and investigate how these improve health and wellbeing
Investigate how foods are marketed to children through advertising, supermarket placement and packaging, and evaluate whether these messages promote healthy choices
Compare a community health practice from a First Nations Australian or Asian Australian cultural context with a familiar practice and discuss similarities and differences in health purpose
elaborations: identifying poison labels and medicine packaging and understanding to ask an adult before taking medicines
discussing how eating a variety of fresh foods can influence health and wellbeing by using The Australian Guide to Healthy Eating
investigating how foods are marketed and promoted to children through advertisements in online spaces, promotion in supermarkets, and labelling and packaging

exploring sustainable practices that students can implement in the classroom to improve the health and wellbeing of the class, such as composting food waste, creating an edible garden and reducing single-use plastics
creating rules and applying them at school and home to implement healthy and manageable practices with their use of digital tools
